subject: renege causing resource to be released?

messages.author: 7840f0c79a42cce9
messages.subject: renege causing resource to be released?
parts:
I've been tearing my hair out all day chasing a bug in my code, but I think it's me misunderstanding r-simmer.

It's a bit lengthy to include the code here, but basically when a patient needs to change ward then they try to seize a new one before releasing the old one.
The patient may end up queuing for the new ward, and I use renege_in() to stop them queueing forever, and to record markers of patients who've been "stuck" on the old ward.
However, when the renege triggers, it appears to release all resources held by the patient - ie they lose their original bed.
Is there any way to avoid this behaviour?

I can probably generate a minimal example now I understand it.

tom

messages.author: 7840f0c79a42cce9
messages.subject: Re: renege causing resource to be released?
parts:
Minimal example:

library(simmer)
env<-simmer()

    patientA <- trajectory("fill ward A") %>%
      seize("wardA") %>%
      timeout(40) %>%
      release("wardA")
   
    patientB <- trajectory("fill ward B") %>%
      seize("wardB") %>%
      timeout(40) %>%
      release("wardB")
   
    log_failure<-trajectory("log failure") %>%
      log_("delay changing wards") %>%
      rollback(2)
   
    patientC <- trajectory("which ward") %>%
      seize("wardA") %>%
      timeout(5) %>%
      renege_in(10,out=log_failure) %>%
      seize("wardB") %>%
      renege_abort() %>%
      release("wardA") %>%
      timeout(40) %>%
      release("wardB")
   
   
    env %>%
    add_resource("wardA",20) %>%
    add_resource("wardB",30) %>%
    add_generator("patientA", patientA, function() {c(rep(0.1,19),-1)}) %>%
    add_generator("patientB", patientB, function() {c(rep(0.1,31),-1)}) %>%
    add_generator("patientC",patientC, at(10)) %>%
    run(80)
 
   
## results in: 'wardA' not previously seized

messages.author: 0f5b7adb7e70bd8b
messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] renege causing resource to be released?
parts:
On Thu, 18 Jul 2019 at 20:39, Tom Lawton <t...@t-lawton.org> wrote:
>
> I've been tearing my hair out all day chasing a bug in my code, but I think it's me misunderstanding r-simmer.
>
> It's a bit lengthy to include the code here, but basically when a patient needs to change ward then they try to seize a new one before releasing the old one.
> The patient may end up queuing for the new ward, and I use renege_in() to stop them queueing forever, and to record markers of patients who've been "stuck" on the old ward.
> However, when the renege triggers, it appears to release all resources held by the patient - ie they lose their original bed.
> Is there any way to avoid this behaviour?

Not at the moment. Reneging activities return all the resources held,
because they are, in principle, designed to completely leave the
system. But I can see the value of just releasing the one in which the
arrival is enqueued. I'll open an issue to track this feature request.

In the meantime, as a workaround, you can

- seize resource A
- decrease capacity of resource A
- release resource A
- set renege_in
- seize resource B (enqueued)
...
- increase capacity of resource A (when you want to release A)

In this way, if reneging is triggered, the arrival still effectively
has resource A seized, because you didn't increase the capacity yet.
You have to take this into account in your analyses though.

Iñaki

messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] renege causing resource to be released?
parts:
On Sat, 20 Jul 2019, 14:14 Iñaki Ucar, <iu...@fedoraproject.org> wrote:
I can see the value of just releasing the one in which the
arrival is enqueued. I'll open an issue to track this feature request.

Thanks. I've had a go at doing this by adding a flag to the renege_in call, but it crashes every time. Presumably because I'm not accounting for the resource it's currently enqueued in. 

For the moment I'm just avoiding reneging, which only affects statistics at present, but in future I can see a need to try to seize a different resource if a patient has been waiting too long. (eg when a patient needs to leave ICU and is waiting for a normal ward bed to go to, they may end up waiting so long that they can just go straight home!) 

Tom
